answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth came from Castle Dracula to Whitby and were consigned to Billington's, then delivered to the old chapel at Carfax (the Count's London base). Twenty-one were later removed: nine to a house in Piccadilly and twelve to Bermondsey and Mile End (six each). Twenty-nine stayed at Carfax. The party destroyed the Carfax boxes and the Bermondsey and Mile End ones; at Piccadilly eight of the nine were found, one was missing.

First mentioned on 26 July 1893 by Mina Murray, in her journal: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep'. Mina's entry implies an earlier habit, but no earlier mention of it is in the store.
Of Lucy's nine narrated entries (letters and diary entries), only the diary entry of 12 September 1893 (e0106) never mentions Arthur. The other eight do.

Four transfusions, in order: (1) 7 Sept, Arthur Holmwood; (2) 10 Sept, Dr. Seward ('friend John'); (3) 13 Sept, Van Helsing, who said 'I shall provide' while Seward operated (donor inferred from that line); (4) 18 Sept, Quincey Morris ('A brave man's blood is the best thing on this earth'). Quincey's count of 'the blood of four strong men' agrees.

The garlic came from Haarlem: a large parcel from abroad, sent by Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool, who grew the herb in his glasshouses there. It arrived at Hillingham on 11 Sept 1893. Van Helsing arranged it: he made the wreath for Lucy's neck, fastened the windows and rubbed the flowers round the sashes and door jambs, and had Seward help him deck the room. Lucy later notes a boxful arriving from Haarlem each day.

Earliest in the store: 5 May 1893, in Jonathan Harker's journal, in Transylvania, where he notes the Slovak and Servian for 'either were-wolf or vampire' and resolves to ask the Count about the superstitions.

One document in the store is written by him: a letter of 25 May 1893 from Quincey P. Morris to Hon. Arthur Holmwood, inviting Arthur to his camp-fire, signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. Seward's diary of 26 Sept says 'Quincey wrote me a line too', but that note is not in the store.

experience: The top-level --help was the most useful part: it names grep, list and read, explains that grep and list are exact and that --by-entry works on whole letters and days, and gives a count line ('43 passages match (26 entries)'), which made it easy to see how much each pattern caught. Searching was less useful for these questions. For Q1 the top hits were mostly passages that mention boxes only in passing, and the exact grep found the counts. The grep pattern 'Yours' matched 340 passages, because the match is case-insensitive and the word is common, so I needed a narrower pattern. The --source filter matches the narrator, so letters from Lucy show up under her name; it would help if the help said whether --source also covers letters where she is the recipient. On Q7 a search gave a 'WARNING CONTINUES' exception telling me to read the surrounding parts. The 'around' command handles that, but the warning did not say which part would change the answer. I wished the output had said which entries are the document's own writing versus quoted by someone else, and whether a passage is one part of a longer entry, which is only visible in the 'part n/m' header. Transfusion donors are not stated in one place; I had to assemble them from several diary passages, and two of the four donors are inferred.
